{{Short description|Statistical bias}}
'''Acquiescence bias''', also known as '''agreement bias''',<ref name="Baron-Epel 543–548">{{Cite journal|last1=Baron-Epel|first1=Orna|last2=Kaplan|first2=Giora|last3=Weinstein|first3=Ruth|last4=Green|first4=Manfred S.|date=October 2010|title=Extreme and acquiescence bias in a bi-ethnic population|journal=European Journal of Public Health|volume=20|issue=5|pages=543–548|doi=10.1093/eurpub/ckq052|issn=1464-360X|pmid=20439322|doi-access=free}}</ref> is a category of [[response bias]] common to [[Sample survey|survey]] research<ref name="Kuru 82–92">{{Cite journal|last1=Kuru|first1=Ozan|last2=Pasek|first2=Josh|date=2016-04-01|title=Improving social media measurement in surveys: Avoiding acquiescence bias in Facebook research|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563215302788|journal=Computers in Human Behavior|language=en|volume=57|pages=82–92|doi=10.1016/j.chb.2015.12.008|issn=0747-5632|url-access=subscription}}</ref> in which respondents have a tendency to select a positive response option<ref name="Baron-Epel 543–548"/><ref name="Krosnick 537–567">{{Cite journal|last=Krosnick|first=Jon A.|date=February 1999|title=Survey Research |journal=[[Annual Review of Psychology]]|language=en|volume=50|issue=1|pages=537–567|doi=10.1146/annurev.psych.50.1.537|pmid=15012463|issn=0066-4308}}</ref> or indicate a positive connotation disproportionately more frequently.<ref name="Kuru 82–92"/><ref name="Watson">{{cite journal|last1=Watson|first1=Dorothy|date=1992|title=Correcting for Acquiescent Response Bias in the Absence of a Balanced Scale: An Application to Class Consciousness|journal=Sociological Methods & Research|volume=21|issue=1|pages=52–88|doi=10.1177/0049124192021001003|s2cid=122977362 }}</ref><ref name="Psychlopedia">{{Cite web |url=http://www.psych-it.com.au/Psychlopedia/article.asp?id=154 |last=Moss |first=Simon |date=2008 |title=Acquiescence bias |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110218193248/http://www.psych-it.com.au/Psychlopedia/article.asp?id=154 |archive-date=2011-02-18 |access-date=2010-07-19}}</ref> Respondents do so without considering the content<ref name="Krosnick 537–567"/> of the question or their 'true' preference.<ref name="Baron-Epel 543–548"/> Acquiescence is sometimes referred to as "yea-saying" and is the tendency of a respondent to agree with a statement when in doubt. Questions affected by acquiescence bias take the following format: a stimulus in the form of a statement is presented, followed by 'agree/disagree,' 'yes/no' or 'true/false' response options.<ref name="Kuru 82–92"/><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.oxfordhandbooks.com/view/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199235476.001.0001/oxfordhb-9780199235476-e-3 |title=Optimizing Survey Questionnaire Design in Political Science|last1=Pasek|first1=Josh|last2=Krosnick|first2=Jon A.|editor1-first=Jan E. |editor1-last=Leighley |date=2010-02-25|website=The Oxford Handbook of American Elections and Political Behavior|language=en|doi=10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199235476.001.0001|isbn=9780199235476|access-date=2020-04-14}}</ref> For example, a respondent might be presented with the statement "gardening makes me feel happy," and would then be expected to select either 'agree' or 'disagree.'  Such question formats are favoured by both survey designers and respondents because they are straightforward to produce and respond to.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567"/><ref name=":0" /> The bias is particularly prevalent in the case of surveys or questionnaires that employ [[truism]]s as the stimuli, such as: "It is better to give than to receive" or "Never a lender nor a borrower be". Acquiescence bias can introduce systematic errors that affect the [[Validity (statistics)|validity]] of research by confounding attitudes and behaviours with the general tendency to agree, which can result in misguided inference.<ref name="Kuru 82–92" /> Research suggests that the proportion of respondents who carry out this behaviour is between 10% and 20%.<ref name="Kuru 82–92" />

== Causes ==

=== Agreeableness ===
{{main|Agreeableness}}
A prominent [[psychological]] explanation attributes acquiescence bias to [[social norm]]s that encourage agreeable behaviour.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" /><ref name=":0" /> Evidence indicates that respondents approach surveys as though they are common [[conversation]]s.<ref name="Kuru 82–92" /> A consequence of this is that the conventions that govern conversations influence the interpretation of survey questions and responses to them. Accordingly, pressure to [[conformity|conform]] to such norms and conventions prompts people to agree with stimulus statements. Based on research into the [[Big Five personality traits|"Big Five" personality traits]], individuals are predisposed to agreeable behaviour to differing degrees.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" />

=== Perceived authority of the interviewer ===
An explanation favoured by [[sociology|sociologists]] is that acquiescence bias is a product of the combination of the inclination to yield to the opinions of high [[authority]] individuals, and respondents' perception of the researcher/ interviewer as having higher authority.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Kuru 82–92" /> According to this explanation, when selecting answers, a tendency to agree with statements made by the interviewer arises from the respondent's intention of being polite or respectful.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" /> In support of this, there is evidence that indicates that respondents of lower social status acquiesce more frequently than respondents of higher social status.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" /> However, several studies have failed to replicate this finding.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" />

=== Satisficing ===
Acquiescence bias is proposed to be a product of '[[satisficing]]' behaviour.<ref name="Kuru 82–92" /> 'Satisficing' sees respondents select responses that are satisfactory or good enough, rather than engage in 'optimizing,' which produces best possible selection. This is done to conserve cognitive energy.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" />

==== Four-stage model of the response process ====
Roger Tourangeau, [[Lance Rips|Lance J. Rips]], Kenneth Rasinski have developed a [[cognitive model]] that proposes four stages to the process of survey response selection. Each stage entails several specific [[cognitive processes]]. For example, the Comprehension stage entails paying attention to a question or instruction set. They propose that some cognitive processes are required in order to select an answer whereas others serve as optional aids. A respondent's decision of which processes to employ from the model is determined by a number of influences, notably speed and precision.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|title=The Psychology of Survey Response|last1=Tourangeau|first1=Roger|last2=Rips|first2=Lance J.|date=March 2000|language=en|last3=Rasinski|first3=Kenneth|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511819322|isbn=9780521572460}}</ref>

The four stages:

* Comprehension – understanding the question and the information required.<ref name=":4" />
* Retrieval (for factual questions) – remembering or calling to mind the appropriate information.<ref name=":4" />
* Judgement (for factual questions) – the processing of recalled information to form judgements.<ref name=":4" />
* Selection – choosing and communicating an answer. Two sets of processes have been proposed: translating a judgement into the scales provided, and revising the response based on factors such as 'consistency'.<ref name=":4" />

Survey [[response effect]]s can arise at any stage of the response process.<ref name=":4" /><ref name="Baron-Epel 543–548" />

==== Strong and weak satisficing ====
Two forms of 'satisficing' have been proposed:<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" />

* ''Weak satisficing'':  Respondents still execute all four stages of the 'Four stage model of the response process.' However, the stages are carried out less rigorously, which results in the output being satisfactory rather than highly accurate. An example of weak satisficing is a respondent who doesn't search their memory as deeply as possible. This would lead to acquiescence if the respondent only scanned their memory for information supporting the positive response option.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" />
* ''Strong satisficing'': Respondents implement a surface-level approach to answering the question by omitting the 'Retrieval' and 'Judgement' stages and only engaging in 'Comprehension' and 'Selection.' The respondent does not access any internal cognitive resources concerning the construct of interest for the question. A mechanism of selecting an appropriate answer may instead involve interpreting external cues such as question-wording. Following the [[social convention]] of agreeing is one alternative mechanism that would lead to Acquiescence bias.<ref name="Krosnick 537–567" />

== Solutions ==

=== Balanced scales ===
This approach involves the modification of scales to include an equal ratio of positively and negatively framed items.<ref name="Baron-Epel 543–548" /> In other words, a particular construct is assessed using conflicting stimulus statements.<ref name="Kuru 82–92" /> For example, in trying to assess depression it would be a good idea to also include items assessing happiness and contentedness, etc. (reversed-keyed items), in addition to the usual depressive content.<ref name="EriksonTedin">{{cite book |last1=Erikson |first1=Robert S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NLXMCgAAQBAJ&pg=PT85 |title=American Public Opinion: Its Origins, Content and Impact|last2=Tedin|first2=Kent L.|date=2015|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781317350385|language=en}}
</ref> The rationale is that such reverse-coded items force respondents to engage consciously and deliberately with survey questions, rather than automatically.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Podsakoff|first1=Philip M.|last2=MacKenzie|first2=Scott B.|last3=Lee|first3=Jeong-Yeon|last4=Podsakoff|first4=Nathan P.|date=Oct 2003|title=Common method biases in behavioral research: a critical review of the literature and recommended remedies|journal=The Journal of Applied Psychology|volume=88|issue=5|pages=879–903 |doi=10.1037/0021-9010.88.5.879|issn=0021-9010|pmid=14516251|hdl=2027.42/147112|s2cid=5281538 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> While this technique has been shown to minimise a construct's relationship with acquiescence bias,<ref name="Kuru 82–92" /> it is imperfect in that respondents continue to provide responses biased by acquiescence.<ref name="Baron-Epel 543–548" />

[[Douglas N. Jackson]] demonstrated acquiescence responding on the [[California F-scale]] (a measure of authoritarianism), which contains such truisms. He created a reverse-keyed version of the California F-scale where all the items were the opposite in meaning (see the two previous examples for a pair of such contradictory statements). He administered both the original and reverse-keyed versions of the California F-scale to the same group of respondents. One would expect that the correlation between these two scales to be negative, but there was a high, positive correlation. Jackson interpreted this as evidence of acquiescence responding. Respondents were merely being agreeable to the statements, regardless of the content.

In such cases, the only effect of the technique is in moving individuals from the positive pole of the scale to the midpoint which, it is argued, achieves nothing.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Kuru 82–92" />

=== Statistical correctives ===
The use of two techniques has been proposed to separate out acquiescence bias from constructs of interest: [[Factor analysis]], and Ipsatization.<ref name="Kuru 82–92" />

Jackson and Messick, using factor analysis, also demonstrated that the two main factors explaining the majority of response variation on the [[Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory]] (MMPI) were for social desirability and acquiescence responding<ref name="Messick">{{cite journal|last1=Messick|first1=Samuel|last2=Jackson|first2=Douglas N.|date=1961|title=Acquiescence and the factorial interpretation of the MMPI.|journal=Psychological Bulletin|volume=58|issue=4|pages=299–304|doi=10.1037/h0043979|pmid=13769793}}</ref> (this would also hold true for the revised MMPI-2).

=== Question choice ===
Some researchers have denounced the use of 'agree/disagree' scales (including 'yes/no' and 'true/false' variations) and call for the use of question types that aren't as susceptible to acquiescence bias.<ref name="Kuru 82–92" />

One alternative is 'item-specific' (IS) questions.<ref name="Kuru 82–92" /> Instead of providing a statement and 'agree/disagree' response option, the statement is transformed into a direct question and response options present a range that captures the extremities of an attitude or behaviour. For example, the statement 'I like the colour blue,' is transformed into 'do you like the colour blue?' with response options ranging from 'not at all' to 'very much.' Proponents of this solution reason that  'agree/disagree' scales demand excess cognitive resources. In many cases, a response to the direct question is a pre-requisite to providing an 'agree/disagree' choice; a person first responds to 'how often do I feel like starting a new hobby?' when presented with the statement 'I regularly feel like starting a new hobby.' There is, therefore, an additional process of translation onto the 'agree/disagree' scale.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Kuru 82–92" />
